processing: A prepared drink: egg yolk is whipped with sugar or condensed milk in a glass, hot black tea is stirred in gradually, and calamondin juice may finish it.
harvest_season: Not tied to a season; it is made to order from everyday black tea all year.
appearance_dry: Not a dry product; the base is ordinary black tea, sometimes in fine or powdered form.
appearance_liquor: An opaque, creamy brown that can settle into layers, with foam on top, a pale middle and brown below.
appearance_wet: No leaf is served in the glass.
taste_profile: Rich and custard-like, very sweet, with strong tea underneath and a sharp lift when citrus is added.

brewing.notes: Whisk one yolk with two spoons of sugar or condensed milk until pale and thick, then pour the hot tea in slowly while stirring. Finish with calamondin or lime to taste.

vintage_note: It is not sold by year or season. It is made to order in lapau, traditional stalls and Padang restaurants. The tea going into it is everyday black tea, so freshness of the egg matters more than any harvest.
description:
Teh talua, or egg tea, is the sweet, foamy tea drink of the Minangkabau of West Sumatra. Egg yolk gives it its body, and in Indonesian it is called teh telur or teh telor.

The yolk, from a chicken or less often a duck, is beaten with sugar or condensed milk right in the glass until it turns into a thick batter. Hot tea goes in gradually while stirring, which is what stops the yolk from scrambling. Traditionally a small whisk tied from dried palm-leaf ribs does the beating.

The result tastes more like a warm custard than a cup of tea. Calamondin juice is the classic finish, added to taste to take away any eggy smell, and it brightens the sweetness as well.

Look for it at lapau, traditional Minangkabau stalls, and in Padang restaurants, where it is often drunk for energy for work. Recipes differ, and some add ginger or spices.
history:
Teh talua belongs to Minangkabau cooking. Among the Minangkabau it is held that the drink was once for the local aristocracy, when tea was a costly import, and spread more widely after large plantations were laid out in West Sumatra in the first third of the 20th century. That is an oral account, not a dated record.

It remains most popular in West Sumatra and in Minangkabau areas of Bengkulu, Jambi, Riau and North Sumatra, and has travelled elsewhere in Indonesia with Minangkabau migration and Padang food. Locals also regard it as healthy, especially for men.
